title: Sum of Matrix After Queries
statement:
Start from an `n x n` grid in which every cell holds 0 (rows and columns are numbered from 0). Apply the entries of `queries` one after another, where `queries[i] = [type_i, index_i, val_i]`:

- `type_i == 0`: every cell of row `index_i` becomes `val_i`, replacing whatever it held.
- `type_i == 1`: every cell of column `index_i` becomes `val_i`, replacing whatever it held.

Once every query has been applied, return the total of all `n * n` cells.
notes:
## Intuition

Filling the grid query by query costs O(n) per query and O(n²) memory. Look at it backwards instead: the last query that touches a row or column decides the cells it still owns, and every earlier query on that same line is fully overwritten. Walking the queries from the end, a row query only owns the cells in columns that no later column query has claimed yet, and the same holds with rows and columns swapped. Two sets of already-claimed lines are all you need.

## Approach

1. Keep `seenRows` and `seenCols`, the lines already decided by later queries, and a running `total`.
2. Walk `queries` from the last one to the first.
3. A row query on a row not yet in `seenRows` claims it and adds `val` once for every column that is still free: `n - seenCols.size` cells.
4. A column query on a fresh column does the same with `n - seenRows.size` free cells.
5. A query on a line already seen changes nothing in the final grid, so it is skipped.
6. Return `total`.

## Example 1, step by step

`n = 3`, read backwards:

- `[1,0,4]`: column 0 is new, no row is claimed, so `4 * 3 = 12` and `total = 12`.
- `[0,2,3]`: row 2 is new, one column is claimed, so `3 * 2 = 6` and `total = 18`.
- `[1,2,2]`: column 2 is new, one row is claimed, so `2 * 2 = 4` and `total = 22`.
- `[0,0,1]`: row 0 is new, two columns are claimed, so `1 * 1 = 1` and `total = 23`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(q), one constant-time set check per query.
- Space: O(min(n, q)) for the two sets.

## Pitfalls

- Going forwards and subtracting overwritten values gets tangled fast; going backwards means nothing is ever undone.
- Skip a repeated line entirely: an earlier query on a claimed row must not add anything.
- The answer can reach 10^13, beyond 32-bit integers (use `long` in Java and C).

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `seenRows` | rows already set by a later query |
| `seenCols` | columns already set by a later query |
| `total` | sum of the cells decided so far |
| `type`, `index`, `val` | the current query's fields |

narration.2: Rows that a later query has already fixed for good.
narration.3: Columns that a later query has already fixed for good.
narration.4: Sum of all cells decided so far.
narration.6: Walk the queries from last to first, because the latest write to a line wins.
narration.8: A row query matters only if no later query already fixed this row.
narration.9: Claim the row so earlier queries on it are ignored.
narration.10: Its value lands on every column that no later column query has taken.
narration.11: A column query matters only if no later query already fixed this column.
narration.13: Its value lands on every row that no later row query has taken.
narration.16: Every cell has been counted exactly once; return the sum.
